Name: safety_drift_anchor
Title: Safety Drift and Restoring Forces: Predicting and Preventing Multi-Turn Jailbreaks by Modeling Representation Trajectories
Short Hypothesis: Building on the established finding that multi-turn jailbreaks (e.g., Crescendo) succeed by slowly dragging a request's internal harmfulness representation into a benign region across turns, we advance a predictive, dynamical treatment. We hypothesize that (1) the velocity and direction of this drift across turns is a robust, attack-agnostic early-warning predictor of an impending jailbreak several turns before the model actually complies, and (2) applying a lightweight per-turn 'restoring force' that re-anchors each new turn's residual-stream representation toward the harmfulness geometry established at the conversation's start prevents the drift and defeats multi-turn attacks without hurting benign multi-turn utility.
Related Work: Prior mechanistic work on multi-turn jailbreaks establishes the phenomenon but not a predictive/dynamical treatment. Aggarwal et al. (2025, 'A Representation Engineering Perspective on Multi-Turn Jailbreaks') show Crescendo makes final harmful tokens *represented as benign*, with drift increasing in the number of turns and driven mainly by user prompts. DEEPALIGN (2025) shows separability decays *within* a single generation and steers at generation midpoint, not across turns. X-Boundary (2025) reshapes the safe/harmful boundary via training. Attention-based works (Attention Slipping 2025; Feint and Attack 2024) explain per-query attention diversion. Neural-barrier-function control (Steering Dialogue Dynamics 2025) learns a black-box state-space safety predictor. Per-turn detectors (BIID 2025; SafeProbing 2026) classify each turn independently. Our proposal is distinct in three ways: (i) it is the first to model safety representation as a *trajectory* and use its drift velocity as a *predictive early-warning* signal (forecasting jailbreak several turns ahead), rather than classifying the current turn; (ii) it introduces an interpretable *restoring-force* intervention that re-anchors each turn to the first-turn harmfulness geometry, directly countering the drift mechanism rather than sharpening attention or moving a global boundary; (iii) it explicitly separates malicious drift from benign topic drift, so restoring forces do not degrade legitimate multi-turn conversations. Concretely, our delta over Aggarwal et al. is not discovering benign drift but converting it into a predictive signal -- the first representation-dynamics treatment that uses drift velocity for turns-ahead forecasting -- and over black-box barrier-function control (Steering Dialogue Dynamics) our forecasting and intervention are interpretable, training-free, and operate directly on the harmfulness representation rather than a learned latent state.
Abstract: Safety-aligned LLMs reliably refuse single harmful requests yet fall to multi-turn attacks like Crescendo, which incrementally steer the conversation until the model complies. Recent mechanistic work shows the cause: as turns accumulate, the model's internal representation of an ultimately-harmful request drifts into a benign region of activation space. We recast multi-turn safety as a dynamical-systems problem over the conversation trajectory. First, we characterize *safety drift*: at each turn we project the residual stream onto a fixed harmfulness direction extracted from single-turn contrasts and track its value, velocity (turn-to-turn change), and cumulative displacement. We hypothesize the drift velocity is a strong, attack-agnostic early-warning signal that forecasts a jailbreak several turns before compliance, and that malicious drift is geometrically distinguishable from benign topic drift. Second, we introduce a *restoring-force* intervention: at each new turn we add a small activation-space correction that pulls the representation back toward the harmfulness geometry anchored at turn one, counteracting the accumulating benign pull without additional training. We evaluate on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B against Crescendo, ActorAttack, and MSJ multi-turn attacks, plus benign multi-turn dialogues from MT-Bench and topic-drifting benign conversations. Metrics: turns-ahead prediction AUROC/lead-time, multi-turn attack success rate, benign multi-turn utility, and over-refusal. We expect drift velocity to predict jailbreaks with several turns of lead time and restoring forces to slash multi-turn attack success while preserving benign multi-turn helpfulness, offering an interpretable, training-free defense targeted at the actual mechanism of multi-turn attacks. The method needs only white-box residual-stream access and one projection per turn, making it a cheap online monitor; and even as a pure measurement, showing that pre-compliance drift velocity forecasts jailbreaks would be a standalone scientific contribution independent of the defense's success.
Experiments:
Models throughout: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-IT, all frozen (the method reads and edits activations; no weight training). The harmfulness direction is extracted per model by difference-in-means on single-turn harmful vs. harmless prompts at each layer; the extraction layer is chosen by held-out single-turn probe AUROC and its causal validity confirmed by single-turn steering (a first-token refusal-rate shift of >=20 points when added/subtracted). "Drift" at turn t is the projection p_t of the final-prompt-token residual stream onto this direction; velocity is p_t - p_{t-1}; displacement is p_t - p_1.

Experiment 1 (H1 — drift velocity is an attack-agnostic early-warning predictor of multi-turn jailbreaks). Tests whether the turn-to-turn drift toward the benign region forecasts compliance several turns ahead and whether malicious drift is geometrically distinct from benign topic drift. Data (constructed from existing sources): 100 harmful goals sampled from HarmBench (400 standard) and StrongREJECT (313), each attacked by three automated multi-turn attackers — Crescendo, ActorAttack, and MSJ/many-shot — on each frozen model, keeping the full turn-by-turn activation trace and the turn at which the judge first marks compliance; 80 benign multi-turn conversations from MT-Bench; and 100 constructed benign topic-drift conversations (start on one subject, gradually change subject over turns) to supply a hard benign negative. We use all attack traces; goals are capped at 100 (not the full pools) to keep the number of multi-turn rollouts affordable. Predictor: a logistic classifier on drift features (value, velocity, curvature over a sliding window of k turns) trained on Crescendo traces and tested on ActorAttack and MSJ (held-out attackers), 5 seeds. Baselines: a per-turn harmfulness probe with no dynamics (BIID-style), Llama-Guard-3 applied per turn, and an attention-slipping metric. Decisive metric first: mean lead-time (turns between the alarm firing at 1% FPR and actual compliance) on held-out attackers; then AUROC and TPR@1%FPR; then malicious-vs-benign-topic-drift AUROC. Convincing result: mean lead-time >=2 turns with held-out-attacker AUROC >=0.85, beating the per-turn probe by >=0.10 AUROC, and benign topic-drift stays low-projection so the malicious-vs-benign classifier reaches AUROC >=0.85 (drift is distinguishable, guarding against over-refusal). Indecision band (before data): AUROC in [0.70, 0.85] or lead-time in [0.5, 2] turns is weak early warning — H1 holds only as a near-compliance detector, and the restoring force below must then be always-on rather than alarm-gated; benign-vs-malicious AUROC in [0.70, 0.85] means partial separability with residual over-refusal risk. Negative result: AUROC <0.70 or lead-time <0.5 turn (the alarm fires only at compliance) means drift velocity carries no early-warning signal and H1 is unsupported.

Experiment 2 (H2 — a per-turn restoring force defeats multi-turn attacks without hurting benign multi-turn utility). Tests whether re-anchoring each new turn toward the turn-1 harmfulness geometry blocks drift-based attacks while preserving benign multi-turn helpfulness. Method: at each new turn t add v_t = beta*(p_1 - p_t)*dhat to the residual stream at the chosen layer, optionally gated on the Experiment 1 drift alarm; dhat is the unit harmfulness direction, beta a scalar gain swept to trace the safety-utility Pareto; frozen models, no training. Data: the same 100-goal multi-turn attack rollouts (Crescendo, ActorAttack, MSJ) for attack success; MT-Bench (80) and AlpacaEval (805) for benign multi-turn and single-turn utility; MMLU (2,000-question fixed subset) for single-turn capability; XSTest-safe (200) and the 100 benign topic-drift conversations for over-refusal. Systems compared: no defense, restoring force (ours, gated and always-on), X-Boundary, circuit breakers, and Attention Sharpening. Decisive metric first: multi-turn attack success rate (judge, plus execution/key verification on the verifiable subset) vs. no defense; then MT-Bench multi-turn score, over-refusal on the benign topic-drift set, and MMLU. Convincing result: restoring force cuts multi-turn ASR by >=40 absolute points vs. no defense while the MT-Bench multi-turn score drops <=0.3 (on the 10-point scale), benign topic-drift over-refusal rises <=5 points, and MMLU drops <=2 points — matching or beating the three defense baselines on the ASR-vs-utility frontier. Indecision band (before data): ASR reduction in [15, 40] points, or an MT-Bench drop in [0.3, 0.6], means the defense works but at a utility cost that must be weighed — reported as a Pareto point, not a win. Negative result: ASR reduction <15 points, or an MT-Bench drop >0.6, means the restoring force is ineffective or too costly, falsifying H2.

Experiment 3 (H2 — adaptive attacker who suppresses drift velocity). Tests whether an attacker aware of the restoring force, who explicitly minimizes per-turn drift velocity, can still succeed and at what cost. Data: the same 100 harmful goals, attacked by a drift-aware variant of Crescendo that penalizes large per-turn projection changes; frozen defended models from Experiment 2. Decisive metric first: attack success rate and mean turns-to-success under the restoring force vs. the non-adaptive attacker. Convincing result: the adaptive attacker needs >=50% more turns or achieves lower ASR than without the defense (raised attack cost is itself the intended safety outcome). Indecision band (before data): a turns-to-success increase in [10, 50]% is a modest cost increase — reported honestly as limited robustness. Negative result: the adaptive attacker reaches equal ASR with no extra turns, showing the restoring force is trivially evadable.

Experiment 4 (mechanism controls and ablations). Isolates that the forecasting signal and the restoring force are specific to the harmfulness geometry rather than generic dynamics, and pins down design choices under a strict train/validation/test split (fit on Crescendo and one model; report on held-out attackers and models). Using the Experiment 1-2 traces on the three frozen models: (a) anchor-choice ablation -- compare the first-turn anchor against a running-average anchor, a fixed harmful-centroid anchor, and a previous-turn local correction, reporting attack success and benign utility for each; (b) mechanism controls -- replace the harmfulness direction in both the predictor and the restoring force with a matched-L2 random direction and an orthogonal (non-harmfulness semantic) direction of equal norm, expecting forecasting AUROC to fall toward chance and the restoring force to lose most of its ASR reduction; (c) representation-slice ablation -- vary the projected token position (final prompt token vs. last generated token) and the layer around the chosen one. Decisive metric first: the drop in forecasting AUROC and in ASR reduction when the real direction is swapped for the random/orthogonal control. Convincing result: real-direction forecasting AUROC exceeds both controls by >=0.15 and the real restoring force's ASR reduction exceeds the controls by >=20 points, with the first-turn anchor within 5 points of the best alternative anchor. Indecision band (before data): a real-vs-control AUROC gap in [0.05, 0.15] means the signal is partly generic -- reported as such. Negative result: controls match the real direction, showing the effect is generic activation perturbation, not harmfulness-specific.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) A single harmfulness direction may be insufficient; drift may occur in a multi-dimensional subspace, requiring subspace projections. 2) Benign topic drift could resemble malicious drift, causing over-refusal; the benign topic-drift benchmark and gating are designed to test/limit this but may not fully resolve it. 3) The turn-1 anchor assumes the first turn is representative; attacks that open benignly and only later introduce harmful intent (delayed-onset) may weaken the anchor, requiring a running or intent-detected anchor. 4) Restoring forces are activation edits that could degrade fluency or benign multi-turn coherence at high gain. 5) Directions and gains are model-specific and require per-model calibration. 6) Adaptive attackers could co-optimize to keep drift velocity low, though this should increase the number of turns/attack cost, itself a safety gain. 7) Verified harm labels are limited to checkable domains; elsewhere we rely on judges.

Name: em_susceptibility_fingerprint
Title: Misalignment Waiting to Happen: Predicting and Pre-Empting Emergent Misalignment from the Base Model's Pre-Fine-Tuning Geometry
Short Hypothesis: Whether a benign-looking fine-tuning dataset will trigger emergent misalignment (EM) is largely determined BEFORE the practitioner's fine-tuning: it is predictable from (a) how strongly the dataset's activations, in the UNMODIFIED base model, already project onto the pre-existing linear misalignment direction, and (b) how tightly that direction is geometrically coupled to the low-rank update the dataset would induce. We combine these into a cheap 'EM-susceptibility fingerprint' that forecasts post-fine-tuning misalignment per-dataset using only a single forward pass plus one cheap single-batch gradient estimate (i.e. near-training-free, with ZERO practitioner training steps), which is non-obvious given that EM is known to depend on training dynamics. We separate three novelty loci: PREDICTION (the fingerprint), MECHANISM (that base-model coupling between the task update and the misalignment direction governs EM magnitude), and PREVENTION (a one-time, dataset-agnostic Pre-Conditioning edit that decorrelates the task from the misalignment direction). We qualify the strongest claim as a scoped hypothesis: Pre-Conditioning is tested to reduce EM across a bank of later benign fine-tunes, not proven to guarantee alignment for ANY conceivable one. The method may require a low-dimensional misalignment SUBSPACE rather than a single direction; we treat that as part of the method, not a fallback.
Related Work: A wave of 2025-2026 work characterizes emergent misalignment (EM) AFTER fine-tuning: Persona Features (SAE 'toxic persona' feature controls EM), Convergent Linear Representations (a single transferable misalignment direction ablates EM), Emergent-Misalignment-is-Easy (the general solution is lower-loss/more-stable, an inductive-bias argument), Character-as-Latent-Variable (character dispositions drive EM), Re-Emergent Misalignment (EM is erosion of prior alignment along a shared latent direction), and BLOCK-EM (blocks causal features DURING fine-tuning). ALL of these operate on or after the fine-tuned model: they detect, steer, or block EM once training is underway, or explain why the general solution wins after the fact. NONE predict, from the frozen BASE model alone and BEFORE any gradient step, WHICH dataset will trigger EM, nor pre-empt EM with a one-time dataset-agnostic edit applied before the practitioner's fine-tuning. Our contribution is distinct on three counts: (1) a pre-fine-tuning susceptibility fingerprint -- base-model projection onto the misalignment direction plus a cheap single-batch gradient-coupling term, i.e. one forward pass and one gradient estimate with ZERO practitioner training steps -- that forecasts per-dataset EM risk; (2) the causal claim that EM magnitude is governed by the base-model geometric alignment between the task's induced update direction and the pre-existing misalignment direction; (3) a preventive edit that decorrelates these directions once, upfront, tested to keep a bank of later benign fine-tunes aligned (a scoped claim, not a guarantee for every possible fine-tune) — complementary to BLOCK-EM (which needs per-run feature blocking during training) and to post-hoc benign re-alignment.
Abstract: Fine-tuning an aligned LLM on narrow, even benign-looking data can trigger emergent misalignment (EM): broadly 'evil' behavior on unrelated prompts. Recent interpretability work shows EM is mediated by a convergent linear misalignment direction and that the general misaligned solution is an inductive-bias attractor. Yet every existing method acts once training is already underway -- detecting, steering, or blocking EM in the fine-tuned model (e.g. during-training BLOCK-EM, post-hoc direction ablation, early-step probes). We ask a sharper, upstream question those methods cannot answer: can we tell, from the frozen base model and before a single practitioner gradient step, which dataset will cause EM, and can we pre-empt it? We hypothesize that a dataset's EM risk is written into the base model's geometry: it is predicted by (a) how strongly the dataset's activations already project onto the pre-existing misalignment direction and (b) the cosine coupling between the low-rank update the dataset would induce and that misalignment direction. We combine these into a cheap 'EM-susceptibility fingerprint' -- a single forward pass plus one single-batch gradient estimate, with no practitioner training. Zero-step prediction is non-obvious because EM depends on learning rate, epochs, and rank, so we explicitly test recipe robustness. First, we validate that the fingerprint forecasts post-fine-tuning misalignment across many datasets and several model families, beating raw-text-classifier and early-step-probe baselines (Location + prediction). Second, we test causality: experimentally increasing or decreasing the base-model coupling between the task and misalignment directions raises or lowers realized EM, holding task content fixed, with matched-norm random-direction controls and an in-domain-loss specificity check to rule out optimization-difficulty artifacts (Causal Intervention). Third, we introduce Pre-Conditioning: a one-time, dataset-agnostic edit that decorrelates the misalignment direction from the model's learning geometry, evaluated for whether it keeps a BANK of subsequent benign fine-tunes aligned at minimal capability cost -- and stress-tested against the prolonged-fine-tuning regime that defeated BLOCK-EM. A fine-tuning platform or safety team would act on this by screening or curating datasets and optionally shipping a pre-conditioned base, saving the cost of pilot fine-tunes; if the result is null, the field learns to stop seeking static pre-training geometry predictors and focus on training dynamics. We evaluate fingerprint AUROC/lead-time, causal dose-response, and pre-conditioning's EM reduction versus in-domain performance and general utility, benchmarking against BLOCK-EM and post-hoc benign re-alignment.
Experiments: Shared setup (referenced below). Models: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-IT, and Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct (the 14B run is the only >9B experiment; if compute is constrained we cap at <=9B and report the weakened scale claim). The base (pre-practitioner-fine-tune) weights are frozen when computing fingerprints; practitioner fine-tunes use LoRA (rank 8, alpha 16, lr 1e-4, 3 epochs, batch 16, 3 seeds) so all training stays within a single-GPU academic budget. Emergent misalignment (EM) is scored as the misalignment rate on held-out unrelated prompts by an LLM judge, cross-checked by projection onto the misalignment direction; both reported. Shared assets. A general-misalignment direction is extracted per base model via difference-in-means between aligned and misaligned response activations sourced from a small reference EM organism (a rank-1 LoRA insecure-code fine-tune from prior work); we validate it by confirming that ablating it removes EM in that organism, and cross-check with an SAE 'toxic-persona'-style feature where available. A bank of 40 fine-tuning datasets spans known-EM-triggering (insecure code, incorrect medical/financial advice, 'evil-number' data), benign (Alpaca, Dolly, domain SFT), and borderline sets; 40 is chosen so every dataset can be actually fine-tuned and EM-evaluated within budget. Experiment 1 (H1 -- A forward-pass-only fingerprint forecasts per-dataset EM before any training): Tests whether pre-fine-tuning geometry predicts realized EM. Data: the 40 datasets; per dataset, in the FROZEN base model, compute F1 = mean projection of response-token activations onto the misalignment direction, F2 = cosine between the dataset's induced low-rank update direction (from a single-batch gradient / rank-1 LoRA warm-start) and the misalignment direction, and F3 = a logistic combination of F1+F2. Then actually LoRA-fine-tune each dataset and measure realized EM. Systems compared: F1-only, F2-only, F3 vs baselines -- a raw-text harmfulness classifier, first-token loss, and cheap early-step (50-step) EM probes; BLOCK-EM feature-activation-during-training as an upper-bound reference. Decisive metric first: AUROC of F3 for EM-vs-no-EM across datasets (leave-one-dataset-out). Convincing: F3 AUROC >= 0.75 and rank-correlation with EM magnitude (Spearman) >= 0.5, beating the raw-text and first-token baselines and generalizing across model families and held-out datasets, with 0 training steps. Indecision band: AUROC 0.6-0.75 -- a weak screen; reported as suggestive and only recommended as a coarse pre-filter. Negative (AUROC <= 0.6 or no better than raw-text classifier): geometry does not forecast EM before training; reported as a null and the causal/defense claims are down-scoped. Experiment 2 (H2 -- Base-model coupling between the task update and the misalignment direction governs EM magnitude): Causal test. Data: 8 fixed datasets spanning the EM range. Method: holding each dataset's task content constant, (a) project the fine-tuning gradient orthogonal to the misalignment direction (expect reduced EM) and (b) add a small component along the misalignment direction (expect increased EM), sweeping coupling strength for dose-response. Systems compared: manipulated coupling vs a matched-magnitude random-direction control; in-domain task loss as the specificity check. Decisive metric first: change in realized EM rate as coupling is decreased vs increased. Convincing: orthogonalization reduces EM by >= 50% (relative) and added coupling increases it, monotone dose-response, while the random-direction control changes EM < 10% (relative) and in-domain task loss is preserved (within 5% of baseline). Indecision band: 20-50% EM reduction -- partial causation. Negative (< 20%, or the random control equally effective): coupling is not the governing cause (EM may be driven by loss-basin inductive bias independent of this geometry); reported as a null. Experiment 3 (H3 -- One-time dataset-agnostic Pre-Conditioning makes later benign fine-tunes EM-resistant): Tests the preventive edit. Data: apply a single Pre-Conditioning edit to each base model WITHOUT knowledge of the downstream dataset (a lightweight weight edit / regularizing pass that flattens the loss basin along the misalignment direction), then fine-tune each of the EM-triggering datasets. Systems compared: no defense; BLOCK-EM (per-run feature blocking); gradient-orthogonalization-during-training; post-hoc benign re-alignment; Pre-Conditioning. Decisive metric first: EM-rate reduction on the EM-triggering datasets vs the un-pre-conditioned baseline. Convincing: Pre-Conditioning cuts EM by >= 50% (relative) averaged over triggering datasets while keeping in-domain task metrics, MMLU (1000-sample), GSM8K (1000-sample) and MT-Bench (80) within 2 pp / 0.1 points and XSTest over-refusal within 5 pp, using ONE edit that transfers across many downstream datasets; we additionally test the prolonged-fine-tuning regime that defeated BLOCK-EM and check whether Pre-Conditioning delays/prevents re-emergence. Indecision band: 25-50% EM reduction, or capability loss of 2-5 pp -- a usable but costly edit; report the EM/capability Pareto. Negative (< 25% EM reduction, capability loss > 5 pp, or re-emergence under prolonged tuning): a clean decorrelation is not achievable (consistent with entangled safety subspaces); reported as an informative negative. Experiment 4 (H1, supporting -- fingerprint component and robustness ablations): Tests which ingredients matter and how far the fingerprint transfers. Data: the 40 datasets and the extracted directions. Systems compared: F1-only vs F2-only vs F3; misalignment-direction layer and organism source; single-direction vs subspace fingerprint; cross-model-family transfer of one fingerprint. Decisive metric first: leave-one-out AUROC under each ablation. Convincing: F3 >= max(F1, F2) by >= 0.03 AUROC and the fingerprint transfers across families with AUROC drop <= 0.1. Indecision band: F3 within 0.03 of the best single feature -- report that one feature suffices. Negative (a single misalignment direction is insufficient, subspace needed, or no cross-family transfer): reported as scoping the method to per-family re-extraction. Exploratory; supports H1.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The fingerprint may fail if EM risk depends on training dynamics (learning rate, epochs, LoRA rank) not captured by a single-gradient / forward-pass estimate; we include cheap early-step baselines and sweep recipes, but the pre-training-step prediction claim could hold only within a fixed recipe. 2) A single misalignment direction may be insufficient (prior work finds multiple persona features / a low-dimensional subspace); F1/F2 may need a subspace rather than one direction, and re-emergence via alternative features (as BLOCK-EM observed) may also defeat pre-conditioning — the prolonged-fine-tuning test directly probes this. 3) Estimating a dataset's 'induced update direction' cheaply (single-batch gradient) may be a noisy proxy for the full fine-tuning trajectory, weakening F2. 4) Pre-conditioning is the riskiest deliverable: flattening the basin along the misalignment direction could harm legitimate capability or over-suppress benign behaviors (the Pareto sweep and utility evals quantify this), and if the misalignment direction is entangled with general learning components (as 'Safety Subspaces are Not Linearly Distinct' warns), a clean decorrelation may be impossible — an informative negative result. 5) The reference EM organism used to source the misalignment direction may bias the direction toward a specific EM flavor; we mitigate with multiple organisms and SAE cross-checks. 6) Results depend on judge-based EM evaluation, which is noisy; we add direction-projection as a complementary metric. 7) Directions, fingerprints, and edits are model-family-specific and require re-extraction; the 14B experiments are the most resource-heavy and may be restricted to <=9B if needed, weakening the scale claim.

Name: safety_verdict_dilution_anchor
Title: Diluting to Comply: A Length-Dependent Decay Law for Safety Signals in Reasoning Models and a Self-Verdict Re-Injection Defense
Short Hypothesis: In reasoning LLMs the model reaches a correct harmfulness verdict early in its chain-of-thought, but this verdict behaves like a finite 'budget' of safety signal that decays roughly monotonically as more CoT tokens accumulate -- largely independent of whether those tokens are relevant -- so that long reasoning (benign or adversarial) mechanically dilutes the safety signal toward the refusal threshold. We hypothesize (1) this dilution follows an approximate, predictable law in CoT length that unifies benign 'refusal cliff', 'self-jailbreak', and length-based CoT-hijacking attacks as facets of one signal-per-token decay, and (2) a training-free intervention that caches the model's own early self-generated safety verdict and re-injects it at the CoT->output boundary restores refusal without capping reasoning length or hurting problem-solving.
Related Work: Recent work on reasoning-model safety establishes pieces of this picture but not the dilution law or the self-verdict defense. 'Refusal Falls off a Cliff' (2025) shows refusal intention is strong during thinking then collapses at the final tokens and ablates a sparse set of 'refusal suppression heads' — a static, head-centric fix that ignores WHY the collapse scales and does not use the model's own verdict. 'Chain-of-Thought Hijacking' (2025) and H-CoT (2025) show long benign reasoning prepends dilute a low-dimensional safety signal and jailbreak LRMs, but treat this as an attack/descriptive finding, not a quantified length-decay law with a matched defense. 'Self-Jailbreaking' (2025) and 'When Models Outthink Their Safety' (CoG, 2025) show models rationalize away their own risk assessment; CoG is a training framework that backtracks unsafe steps. 'Can We Predict Alignment Before Models Finish Thinking?' (2025) probes CoT activations to MONITOR alignment but does not intervene. ACT (2026) is training-based activation consistency. Our contribution is distinct: (i) we advance and empirically fit a positional/length dilution LAW for the safety signal that mechanistically UNIFIES the refusal cliff, self-jailbreak, and length-based CoT hijacking as the same phenomenon (signal-per-token decay), and (ii) we propose a training-free 'Self-Verdict Anchoring' that extracts the model's OWN early safety conclusion from its CoT activations and re-injects it at the answer boundary, counteracting dilution regardless of reasoning length — unlike head-ablation (static), length caps (utility-destroying), CoG/ACT (training-based), or monitor-only probes. We name the closest baselines explicitly and why none implies the unification: Refusal-Cliff head-ablation is static and does not model why collapse scales with length; CoT-Hijacking/H-CoT report the attack but fit no length-decay law; monitor-only probes forecast alignment without intervening. SVA differs from generic logit/activation steering in that its target is the model's own cached early verdict rather than an externally-fixed refusal direction, and we include a no-op control anchor (re-injecting a matched-norm non-caution vector) to show the effect is the verdict, not generic late-token perturbation.
Abstract: Reasoning LLMs that produce long chains of thought (CoT) are, paradoxically, easier to jailbreak: prepending benign puzzle reasoning or verbose 'educational' framing reliably strips their refusals. Recent mechanistic work has separately reported that refusal intention is strong during thinking but collapses at the answer boundary ('refusal cliff'), that a low-dimensional safety signal gets 'diluted' by long reasoning, and that models rationalize away their own risk assessments. We propose that these are one phenomenon: the model computes a correct harmfulness verdict early, but the safety signal behaves like a finite budget that decays roughly monotonically with the number of CoT tokens, independent of their content, until it falls below the refusal threshold. We (1) test this by probing a harmfulness/caution direction across token positions in the CoT and fitting a decay law as a function of reasoning length, showing benign long CoT, self-jailbreak, and adversarial CoT-hijacking all follow the same decay and that injecting content-free filler tokens alone dilutes the signal and increases compliance. We (2) introduce Self-Verdict Anchoring (SVA), a training-free defense that reads the model's own peak early safety verdict from its CoT activations and re-injects it as an activation anchor at the CoT→output boundary, counteracting length-driven decay without capping reasoning. On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B/Qwen-7B, s1.1, and Qwen3-thinking we evaluate the decay-law fit, attack success under CoT-hijacking/H-CoT/self-jailbreak, over-refusal, and reasoning utility (GSM8K/MATH/GPQA). We expect a robust length-dilution law and SVA to defeat length-based jailbreaks while preserving reasoning performance, outperforming length caps and head-ablation. Operationally, SVA is an inference-time monitor a lab can drop into a reasoning-model safety stack -- a per-token projection plus a boundary nudge -- reducing length-based ASR at fixed reasoning accuracy without a length cap or retraining; it changes inference-time defense rather than training or evaluation policy.
Experiments:
Models throughout: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, and Qwen3-8B in thinking mode, all frozen (the defense edits activations; no training); an optional s1.1-32B run is included only if compute allows and does not gate any conclusion. The "caution" direction is extracted per model by difference-in-means on harmful vs. harmless prompts at chain-of-thought (CoT) token positions over a layer sweep, layer chosen by held-out probe AUROC and causal validity confirmed by ablation (removing it lowers first-token refusal rate on harmful prompts by >=20 points). A prompt's safety signal at CoT position i is the residual stream at i projected onto this direction.

Experiment 1 (H1 — the safety signal follows one length-dilution law that unifies benign long CoT, self-jailbreak, and CoT-hijacking). Tests whether the safety signal decays roughly monotonically with CoT token count independent of content, with a single law across three regimes, and whether content-free filler alone dilutes it. Data: 200 harmful behaviors sampled from HarmBench (400), StrongREJECT (313), and AdvBench (520); three regimes eliciting long CoT — (a) benign verbose reasoning (natural long CoT), (b) self-jailbreak (model spontaneously introduces benign assumptions), (c) adversarial CoT-hijacking / H-CoT (benign-puzzle or "educational" prepends). Content-free control: 100 harmful prompts each run with 0, 100, 300, 600, and 1000 injected semantically irrelevant filler CoT tokens (repeated neutral text/unrelated arithmetic), harmful content held fixed. Method: project the CoT residual onto the caution direction at every token; fit candidate decay laws (linear, exponential, 1/N) of signal vs. token count; compare fitted parameters across the three regimes; replicate the refusal-cliff drop at the CoT→answer boundary and relate its size to the pre-boundary diluted signal predicted by the law; frozen models. Decisive metric first: R^2 of a single decay law fit jointly across the three regimes with shared parameters; then, for the content-free control, the Spearman correlation between filler-token count and compliance rate at fixed harmful content. Convincing result: one law fits all three regimes with R^2 >=0.8 and overlapping parameter confidence intervals across regimes, and filler alone raises compliance monotonically (Spearman rho >=0.6), establishing length-driven, content-independent dilution. Indecision band (before data): joint R^2 in [0.5, 0.8], or regime parameters that only partly overlap, means length matters but content also modulates the signal — the "law" holds approximately and is reported with per-regime parameters. Negative result: joint R^2 <0.5, or filler having no effect (rho <0.3), means there is no length-driven dilution law and H1 is unsupported.

Experiment 2 (H2 — Self-Verdict Anchoring defeats length-based jailbreaks without capping reasoning or hurting problem-solving). Tests whether caching the model's own peak early safety verdict and re-injecting it at the CoT→output boundary restores refusal while preserving reasoning accuracy that length caps sacrifice. Method (SVA): monitor the caution projection over the CoT, cache the peak (early) value and its sign; at the CoT→output boundary (and optionally a sliding set of late positions) add v = beta*(peak - current)*dhat; gated on the cached peak so low-peak (benign) requests are untouched; training-free, one fixed setting per model. Data: attack success on CoT-Hijacking, H-CoT/Malicious-Educator, and self-jailbreak prompts (built on the 200 harmful behaviors), plus standard GCG/AutoDAN/PAIR; over-refusal on XSTest-safe (200) and OR-Bench (500); reasoning utility on GSM8K (1,319 test), MATH-500, GPQA-Diamond (198), and general MT-Bench (80). Systems compared: no defense, hard CoT length cap, refusal-suppression-head ablation (Refusal Cliff), safe-thinking-token prompting, per-turn Llama-Guard-3; ablations sweep anchor strength beta, compare peak-verdict vs. running-mean vs. first-sentence anchor, layer, and boundary-only vs. periodic re-injection. Decisive metric first: length-based attack ASR reduction at matched reasoning accuracy; then over-refusal. Convincing result: SVA cuts CoT-hijacking/H-CoT/self-jailbreak ASR by >=40 points vs. no defense while GSM8K/MATH-500/GPQA-Diamond accuracy drops <=2 points, whereas a length cap achieving comparable ASR reduction drops reasoning accuracy >=10 points; over-refusal rises <=5 points. Indecision band (before data): ASR reduction in [15, 40] points, or a reasoning-accuracy drop in [2, 5] points, means SVA helps but its advantage over length caps is not decisive — reported as a Pareto point. Negative result: ASR reduction <15 points, or a reasoning drop >5 points, means SVA fails or costs too much reasoning, falsifying H2.

Experiment 3 (H2 — adaptive attacker who suppresses the early verdict itself). Tests whether an attacker who targets the cached peak verdict, not just dilutes it, can defeat SVA and at what cost. Data: an adaptive attack on the 200 harmful behaviors that opens with framing designed to keep the early caution projection low (so the cached peak is already compromised), run against SVA-defended models. Decisive metric first: ASR under SVA vs. the non-adaptive length attack; then the attack length/query budget required. Convincing result: to defeat SVA the attacker must suppress the early peak, which either raises the Experiment-1 detection signal or forces shorter/less-effective attacks (>=50% higher budget or lower ASR) — a raised attack cost. Indecision band (before data): a budget increase in [10, 50]% is a modest cost, reported honestly. Negative result: the adaptive attacker matches undefended ASR at no extra cost, showing SVA is bypassed by early-verdict suppression (the failure mode its risk section anticipates).

Experiment 4 (controls separating length from format, and the no-op anchor). Rules out that the decay is a tokenization/format artifact and that SVA is generic late-token steering. Data: the 200 harmful behaviors and the three frozen reasoning models. Length/format controls: repeat the filler-dilution sweep with (a) whitespace/format-only padding vs. semantic filler vs. unrelated-arithmetic filler, matched in token count, and (b) a benign long-context non-safety task (long GSM8K/MATH reasoning) to confirm the caution projection is stable when no safety verdict is at stake. SVA controls: a no-op anchor that re-injects a matched-L2 non-caution (random or orthogonal) vector at the boundary, and an anchor that re-injects a late (already-diluted) value instead of the cached peak. Decisive metric first: whether format-only padding dilutes the signal as much as semantic filler at matched token count (it should not, if the effect is length-of-reasoning rather than raw tokens) and whether the no-op anchor recovers refusal (it should not). Convincing result: semantic/arithmetic filler dilutes >=2x more than format-only padding per token, the benign non-safety task shows no caution decay, and the no-op anchor yields <10 points ASR reduction while SVA yields >=40. Indecision band (before data): format-only padding diluting within [0.5x, 1x] of semantic filler means part of the effect is raw token count -- reported honestly. Negative result: format-only padding diluting as much as semantic filler, or the no-op anchor matching SVA, means the mechanism/defense is not caution-specific.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The decay may not be a clean monotonic function of length; content and length could be entangled, weakening the 'law' — the content-free filler experiment is designed to disentangle this but may show partial effects. 2) Some length-based jailbreaks may also corrupt the EARLY verdict (not just dilute it), in which case the cached peak is already compromised and SVA helps less; the adaptive-attack experiment probes this. 3) A single caution direction may be multi-dimensional across layers, requiring subspace anchoring. 4) Re-injecting a stale early verdict could cause over-refusal when legitimate benign reasoning revises an initially cautious judgment (a benign request that first looks alarming); the over-refusal and gating analyses quantify this. 5) Activation anchoring at high strength may degrade CoT fluency or reasoning coherence; the utility benchmarks and beta Pareto test this. 6) Directions, decay-law parameters, and anchor strengths are model-specific and need per-model calibration. 7) Results may depend on how thinking mode is elicited (open-weights distilled reasoners vs. RL-trained ones); we mitigate by testing multiple model families but cannot cover closed models.

Name: safety_verdict_uncertainty
Title: False Confidence: Jailbreaks Collapse the Model's Uncertainty About Its Own Safety Verdict, and Re-Injecting It Restores Refusal
Short Hypothesis: Aligned LLMs carry a distinct, linearly-readable representation of epistemic uncertainty about their OWN safety verdict ('how sure am I that this request is safe?'), separate from output-token entropy, from the harmfulness-belief direction, and from the refusal-action direction. We hypothesize (1) many jailbreaks succeed not by flipping the harmfulness belief nor merely suppressing refusal, but by artificially COLLAPSING this safety-verdict uncertainty to false confidence, so the model commits to compliance without hedging or reflecting; and (2) a training-free intervention that detects abnormally-collapsed verdict uncertainty and re-injects calibrated uncertainty re-triggers the model's cautious/reflective refusal pathway, defeating jailbreaks with low over-refusal.
Related Work: SIRL/Safety Instincts (2025) observes an entropy GAP (low-entropy refusals vs high-entropy dangerous generation) and turns it into an RL reward; it uses raw output entropy as a training signal and does not isolate a verdict-uncertainty representation or intervene at inference. SCIURus (2025) shows factuality and uncertainty share circuits but studies factual QA, not safety. 'Calibrating Verbal Uncertainty' (2025) finds a linear verbal-uncertainty feature for hallucinations, not safety. 'Confidence is Not Competence' (2025) finds a solvability-belief axis that is causally inert for execution. Zhao et al. (2025) separate harmfulness (belief) from refusal (action). Our proposal introduces a THIRD, previously-unisolated safety object: the model's epistemic uncertainty about its safety verdict (metacognitive confidence in the safe/harmful classification), and advances the causal claim that jailbreaks work by inducing FALSE CONFIDENCE (collapsing this uncertainty) rather than only flipping belief or suppressing refusal. Unlike SIRL (training-based, output entropy), our defense is training-free and re-injects calibrated verdict uncertainty at inference; unlike Latent Guard (harmfulness classifier) it targets the confidence-in-the-verdict axis, which we show distinguishes confident jailbreaks from genuinely ambiguous benign requests. We pre-register the disconfirming outcomes: high alignment (|cosine|>0.6) of verdict-uncertainty with the harmfulness-belief or output-entropy direction, or causal patching failing to transfer, would mean the axis is not a distinct, actionable mechanism -- a result we would report as such.
Abstract: Aligned LLMs refuse single harmful requests but fall to jailbreaks. Two mechanistic accounts dominate: jailbreaks either flip the model's harmfulness belief or suppress its refusal action while leaving the belief intact. We propose a complementary and, we argue, for an identifiable subset of jailbreaks dominant mechanism grounded in metacognition: jailbreaks induce FALSE CONFIDENCE, collapsing the model's uncertainty about its OWN safety verdict so it commits to compliance without the hedging/reflection that normally precedes a refusal. We first isolate a safety-verdict-uncertainty representation using minimal pairs that hold harmfulness content fixed but vary how CONFIDENT the model should be about the safe/harmful classification (clearly-harmful vs clearly-benign vs genuinely-ambiguous requests), extracting a linear verdict-uncertainty direction via difference-in-means and validating it is separable (low cosine) from harmfulness-belief, refusal-action, and raw output-entropy directions. We then test causally whether successful jailbreaks systematically drive this direction toward false confidence (low uncertainty) while the harmfulness belief remains high, using activation patching to show that patching only the collapsed verdict-uncertainty component into a clean run transfers compliance, and re-injecting uncertainty into a jailbroken run restores refusal. Finally we introduce Verdict-Uncertainty Re-injection (VUR), a training-free defense that flags abnormally-collapsed verdict uncertainty (given a still-high harmfulness belief) and adds an activation nudge re-inflating uncertainty, re-triggering cautious refusal. On Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B we measure direction separability, the jailbreak false-confidence signature, causal patching transfer, and VUR's attack-success reduction versus over-refusal (XSTest/OR-Bench) and utility (MMLU/MT-Bench). We expect false confidence to be a robust, attack-agnostic jailbreak signature and VUR to Pareto-dominate belief/refusal-only defenses on genuinely-ambiguous inputs. We separate the scientific contribution (a third jailbreak pathway) from the product-defense contribution (VUR), so that even a negative VUR result contributes a new mechanistic pathway to the jailbreak taxonomy.
Experiments:
Models throughout: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-IT, all frozen (directions are read and the defense edits activations; no training). Four directions are extracted by difference-in-means over a layer sweep, layer chosen per direction by held-out probe AUROC: verdict-uncertainty (confident/clear vs. genuinely-ambiguous requests, at the last instruction token), harmfulness-belief (harmful vs. harmless), refusal-action (post-instruction token, comply vs. refuse), and a raw output-entropy proxy. Projections are standardized to units of standard deviations (SD) over a calibration set.

Experiment 1 (H1 setup — a safety-verdict-uncertainty axis distinct from belief, refusal, and output entropy). Tests whether an epistemic-uncertainty-about-own-verdict direction exists and is separable from the other three. Data (constructed): a minimal-pair set holding request content-type roughly fixed while varying the appropriate confidence in the safety verdict — clearly-harmful (confidently harmful), clearly-benign (confidently safe), and genuinely-ambiguous/dual-use (verdict SHOULD be uncertain, e.g., "how do household chemicals react", "explain how phishing works for training"); ~500 items per category, auto-generated with a 10% hand-checked sample. Method: extract the verdict-uncertainty direction (clear vs. ambiguous) and the other three directions, validate each with probe AUROC on held-out sets, and compute pairwise cosine similarities; frozen models. Decisive metric first: pairwise cosine between verdict-uncertainty and each of harmfulness-belief, refusal-action, and output-entropy; then the verdict-uncertainty probe AUROC on held-out clear-vs-ambiguous items. Convincing result: every verdict-uncertainty pairwise |cosine| <=0.3 and its probe AUROC >=0.85, establishing a distinct, readable axis. Indecision band (before data): a cosine in [0.3, 0.6] with belief or output-entropy means the axis is only partly distinct — the causal test below is expected to be muddier. Negative result: |cosine| >0.6 with harmfulness-belief or output-entropy means verdict-uncertainty is not a separate axis and the hypothesis's premise fails.

Experiment 2 (H1 — successful jailbreaks collapse verdict-uncertainty to false confidence while belief stays high). Tests whether the false-confidence signature is present and dominant across attack families. Data: GCG, AutoDAN, PAIR, and roleplay/DAN attacks (JailbreakBench 100 + HarmBench 100 sampled behaviors) run per model, split into judge-confirmed successes and failures. Method: for successful vs. failed attacks, measure the projection change on all four directions; frozen models. Decisive metric first: the mean verdict-uncertainty shift on successful jailbreaks (toward low/confident, in SD) alongside the belief shift; then whether verdict-uncertainty is the largest-shifting of the four directions and how consistently across families. Convincing result: on the majority of attack families verdict-uncertainty drops >=1.0 SD while harmfulness-belief stays within 0.5 SD, and verdict-uncertainty is the largest-shifting direction (false confidence, not belief flip or mere refusal suppression). Indecision band (before data): a verdict-uncertainty drop in [0.5, 1.0] SD means the signature is present but weak — H1 holds partially and VUR is expected to help less. Negative result: verdict-uncertainty not dropping, or belief itself dropping >=1.0 SD (a belief-flip mechanism), means false confidence does not explain those attacks — recorded as a scope limit (e.g., abliteration-style attacks may fall here).

Experiment 3 (H1 — the verdict-uncertainty collapse is causally responsible for compliance). Tests, via patching, whether the collapsed uncertainty component drives compliance rather than merely correlating (the crucial test given that decodable axes can be causally inert). Data: matched jailbroken-complied vs. clean-refused run pairs on the same behaviors from Experiment 2 (target 200 pairs per model). Method: (a) patch ONLY the collapsed verdict-uncertainty component from a jailbroken run into a clean refused run and measure induced compliance; (b) patch harmfulness-belief alone and refusal-action alone as controls; (c) reverse — re-inject high verdict-uncertainty into a jailbroken run and measure restored refusal; frozen models. Decisive metric first: compliance-transfer rate from patching verdict-uncertainty alone vs. the control patches; then the reverse restored-refusal rate. Convincing result: verdict-uncertainty-only patching induces compliance in >=50% of clean-refused runs while belief-only and refusal-only patches induce <=15%, and re-injecting uncertainty restores refusal in >=50% of jailbroken runs. Indecision band (before data): a verdict-uncertainty transfer rate in [25, 50]% means it is one contributing cause among several — reported as partial, and VUR expected to be partially effective. Negative result: transfer <25% (near the controls) means verdict-uncertainty is causally inert and H1's causal claim fails — an informative negative.

Experiment 4 (H2 — Verdict-Uncertainty Re-injection defeats jailbreaks with low over-refusal on ambiguous inputs). Tests whether re-inflating collapsed uncertainty, gated on a still-high belief, restores refusal while hedging rather than blanket-refusing genuinely-ambiguous requests. Method (VUR): gated on a still-high harmfulness-belief projection, detect abnormally-low verdict-uncertainty and add v = beta*(target_uncertainty - current)*dhat at chosen layer(s); training-free, one fixed setting per model; belief-gating leaves genuinely-benign requests untouched. Data: attack success on GCG/AutoDAN/PAIR/roleplay (judge + verification where possible); over-refusal on XSTest-safe (200), OR-Bench (500), and specifically the genuinely-ambiguous/dual-use set from Experiment 1 (where VUR should hedge/qualify, not refuse); utility on MMLU (2,000-subset), MT-Bench (80), AlpacaEval (805). Systems compared: no defense, refusal-direction steering, harmfulness Latent Guard, SafeSwitch, and SIRL-style output-entropy thresholding; ablations isolate re-injecting uncertainty vs. belief vs. refusal, sweep beta (Pareto), gated vs. always-on, and layer. Decisive metric first: attack-success reduction paired with over-refusal on the ambiguous/dual-use set; then over-refusal on XSTest/OR-Bench and utility. Convincing result: VUR cuts ASR by >=40 points vs. no defense while its over-refusal on the ambiguous set is >=10 points lower than belief/refusal-only defenses at matched ASR, with MMLU drop <=2 points. Indecision band (before data): ASR reduction in [15, 40] points, or an ambiguous-set over-refusal advantage in [3, 10] points, means VUR helps but does not clearly Pareto-dominate — reported as such. Negative result: ASR reduction <15 points, or no over-refusal advantage on ambiguous inputs over belief/refusal-only defenses, means VUR adds nothing and H2 is unsupported.

Experiment 5 (H2 — adaptive attacker who co-suppresses both axes). Tests whether an attacker who jointly keeps verdict-uncertainty low AND harmfulness-belief low can evade the belief-gated VUR, and at what cost. Data: an adaptive attack on the 100 JailbreakBench behaviors optimized to keep both projections low, run against VUR-defended models. Decisive metric first: ASR under VUR vs. the non-adaptive attack; then the query budget required. Convincing result: co-suppressing both axes forces >=50% more queries or yields lower ASR than the undefended baseline (raised attack cost). Indecision band (before data): a query-budget increase in [10, 50]% is a modest cost, reported honestly. Negative result: the adaptive attacker matches undefended ASR at no extra cost, showing VUR is bypassed by joint suppression (the failure its risk section anticipates).

Experiment 6 (identification and behavioral controls). Guards against the verdict-uncertainty axis being generic uncertainty and against VUR being mere induced caution. Data: the Experiment-1 sets and Experiment-3 matched run pairs on the three frozen models. Identification controls: augment cosine separability with partial (residualized) probes for verdict-uncertainty after regressing out harmfulness-belief, refusal-action, and output-entropy, plus subspace/CCA overlap; and projection-removal tests (does removing the verdict-uncertainty component change compliance while removing a matched-norm random component does not). Causal controls: patch a matched-L2 random direction, a generic non-safety uncertainty direction extracted from ambiguous factual-QA (not safety), and sham patches at nearby layers/tokens, all expected to induce <=15% compliance vs. the real verdict-uncertainty patch. Behavioral control: measure whether VUR increases verbosity/hedging on plainly benign tasks (response length and refusal rate on Alpaca/MT-Bench) beyond the intended ambiguous-set hedging. Decisive metric first: residualized verdict-uncertainty probe AUROC and the real-vs-control patch compliance gap; then VUR's benign-task verbosity/refusal change. Convincing result: residualized AUROC >=0.75, the real patch exceeds all controls (random, generic-uncertainty, sham) by >=35 points, and VUR raises benign-task refusal <=3 points and length <=10%. Indecision band (before data): residualized AUROC in [0.6, 0.75], or a generic-uncertainty patch within 10 points of the real patch, means verdict-uncertainty partly overlaps generic uncertainty -- reported as partial specificity. Negative result: the real patch near the controls, or VUR broadly increasing caution on benign tasks, means the axis is generic uncertainty, not a safety-verdict mechanism.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Verdict-uncertainty may not be cleanly separable from harmfulness belief or output entropy; the axes could be entangled, weakening the causal decomposition — the separability and patching experiments directly test this. 2) Constructing minimal pairs that vary appropriate verdict confidence while holding content fixed is delicate; residual confounds (topic, wording) could contaminate the direction. 3) Some jailbreaks (e.g., pure refusal-action suppression via abliteration) may NOT collapse verdict uncertainty, so VUR may help less on those; the per-direction shift analysis quantifies which attacks the mechanism explains. 4) 'Confidence is Not Competence' warns that decodable belief axes can be causally inert; verdict-uncertainty might likewise be non-actionable — the patching experiment is the crucial causal test, and a negative result is itself informative. 5) Re-injecting uncertainty could over-hedge and reduce helpfulness on legitimately confident benign requests; belief-gating and the Pareto sweep quantify this. 6) A single verdict-uncertainty direction may be multi-dimensional, requiring subspace re-injection. 7) Directions and gains are model-specific and need per-model calibration; adaptive attackers co-suppressing both axes remain a threat, though this raises attack cost.

Name: lexical_vs_semantic_safety
Title: Word or Meaning? Disentangling Lexical-Trigger and Semantic-Intent Components of LLM Safety Decisions to Cure Both Over-Refusal and Jailbreaks
Short Hypothesis: An aligned LLM's harmfulness judgment is a sum of two causally separable contributions: a shallow lexical-trigger component (driven by surface tokens like 'kill', 'bomb') and a deep semantic-intent component (driven by the actual meaning of the request). We hypothesize that over-refusal (benign prompts with alarming words) and jailbreaks (harmful requests laundered into innocuous-looking phrasings) are DUAL failures on the SAME axis: over-refusal over-weights the lexical component, jailbreaks exploit the model's over-reliance on lexical cues by removing them while preserving harmful semantics. Reading and re-weighting these two components at inference should reduce both failure modes simultaneously with a single, interpretable, training-free intervention, rather than trading one against the other as threshold-based methods do.
Related Work: Prior work documents safety shortcuts descriptively or fixes only one failure direction. Self-CD/OverKill (2024) shows over-attention to harmful words and contrastively decodes to reduce over-refusal. D-STT (2025) identifies 'safety trigger tokens' and decodes them to defend jailbreaks. Shallow-safety (2024) and Incomplete-Learning (2025) show alignment is first-few-tokens deep. TASA (2025) shows safety is anchored in the template region. MOSR (2025) and RASS (2025) analyze over-refusal via representation boundaries. Zhao et al. (2025) separate harmfulness (belief) from refusal (action). Our contribution is distinct and unifying: (1) we causally decompose the harmfulness BELIEF itself into a lexical-trigger component and a semantic-intent component per token, rather than treating harmfulness as monolithic (Zhao et al.) or attacking only over-attention (Self-CD) or only trigger-defense (D-STT); (2) we advance the concrete, testable claim that over-refusal and jailbreaks are the SAME mechanistic pathology viewed from opposite ends of one lexical-vs-semantic axis, and validate it causally; (3) we build ONE training-free intervention that recomputes the safety decision from the semantic-intent component with the lexical component down-weighted, fixing both directions at once, whereas all prior methods target a single direction and risk trading one failure for the other. Critically, refusal-direction steering and single-threshold guards move one scalar magnitude and therefore cannot separate lexical from semantic contributions to that magnitude; our identification strategy -- matched minimal pairs (meaning-fixed/lexicon-swapped and lexicon-fixed/meaning-swapped) plus trigger-token activation patching -- is what operationalizes the decomposition as a causal measurement, not merely a re-description of known lexical overfitting.
Abstract: Safety-aligned LLMs fail in two seemingly opposite ways: they refuse benign requests that merely contain alarming words (over-refusal), and they comply with harmful requests that have been rephrased to look innocuous (jailbreaks). We argue these are not separate problems but dual manifestations of a single mechanistic confound: the model's harmfulness judgment mixes a shallow lexical-trigger component, driven by surface tokens, with a deeper semantic-intent component, driven by the request's actual meaning. Over-refusal is what happens when the lexical component dominates on benign-but-alarming inputs; many jailbreaks succeed precisely because they strip the lexical triggers the model over-relies on while preserving harmful semantics. We test this hypothesis by causally decomposing the harmfulness direction's activation into lexical and semantic contributions using minimal-pair prompts (same meaning, swapped trigger words; same words, swapped meaning) together with activation patching and attention attribution to localize where lexical vs. semantic harm is computed. We then introduce Semantic-Recompute, a training-free inference intervention that estimates the lexical-trigger contribution to the residual stream and subtracts it, leaving a harmfulness decision grounded in semantic intent. Because it removes the confound rather than shifting a global refusal threshold, a single setting should reduce over-refusal AND increase jailbreak robustness together, escaping the safety-usability trade-off that plagues threshold- or steering-based methods. We evaluate on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B, measuring over-refusal (XSTest, OR-Bench, OKTest), jailbreak robustness (GCG, AutoDAN, PAIR, roleplay, word-substitution attacks), and utility (MMLU, MT-Bench). We expect the lexical/semantic decomposition to be causally validated and Semantic-Recompute to improve both failure modes simultaneously. For deployers this targets the safety-usability trade-off directly -- fewer harmless refusals and less moderation burden without a separate jailbreak-hardening pass -- and we test generalization across three model families and multiple attack types to gauge uptake.
Experiments:
Models throughout: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-IT, all frozen (the intervention edits activations; no training). The harmfulness direction is extracted per model by difference-in-means at the last instruction token over a layer sweep, layer chosen by held-out probe AUROC and causal validity confirmed by single-turn steering (first-token refusal-rate shift >=20 points). A prompt's projection onto this direction is decomposed into a lexical-trigger component and a semantic-intent component using the minimal pairs below.

Experiment 1 (H1 — the lexical-trigger and semantic-intent contributions are causally separable and localizable). Tests whether the harmfulness projection splits into a lexical component (changes when only trigger words change) and a semantic component (changes when only meaning changes) that are near-orthogonal and localizable. Data (constructed): two minimal-pair sets, ~500 pairs each, across HarmBench categories. (a) Same-meaning/swapped-lexicon: a harmful request with explicit trigger words vs. a semantically identical euphemistic/synonym-obfuscated phrasing (isolates the lexical contribution). (b) Same-lexicon/swapped-meaning: benign requests containing trigger words (e.g., "how to kill a Python process") vs. genuinely harmful requests using those words (isolates the semantic contribution). Pairs are generated automatically and spot-checked by hand (we validate a 10% random sample; a pair is discarded if two annotators disagree that meaning/lexicon was held constant). Method: for each pair measure the harmfulness-projection change under lexicon-only vs. meaning-only swaps (component magnitudes per layer); localize with activation patching of trigger-token positions and per-head attention attribution; logit-lens to trace when each commits; frozen models. Decisive metric first: cosine similarity between the mean lexical-swap delta vector and the mean meaning-swap delta vector; then the fraction of the lexical component transferred by patching trigger-token positions. Convincing result: |cosine| <=0.3 (near-orthogonal, separable) and trigger-token patching transfers >=50% of the lexical component, with lexical harm entering in early layers and semantic intent integrated mid-to-late (as attention attribution predicts). Indecision band (before data): |cosine| in [0.3, 0.6] means the components overlap partially — the decomposition is approximate and the intervention below is expected to be imperfect. Negative result: |cosine| >0.6 means lexical and semantic contributions are entangled and not cleanly separable, undercutting the decomposition premise of H1.

Experiment 2 (H1 — over-refusal and jailbreaks are dual failures on the same lexical/semantic axis). Tests whether over-refusal prompts sit at high-lexical/low-semantic and successful jailbreaks at low-lexical/high-semantic, with true-harmful high-both and true-benign low-both. Data: over-refusal prompts from XSTest-safe (200), OR-Bench-Hard-1K (500 sampled), and OKTest (300); successful jailbreaks harvested by running GCG, AutoDAN, PAIR, roleplay, and a word-substitution/euphemism attack on 100 HarmBench behaviors per model (keeping judge-confirmed successes); true-harmful = 100 HarmBench behaviors under direct request; true-benign = 200 Alpaca instructions. Method: place each prompt in the (lexical projection, semantic projection) plane; report the 2D scatter and the macro-F1 of a 2-feature classifier separating the four groups. Decisive metric first: the fraction of over-refusal prompts with below-median semantic projection and the fraction of successful jailbreaks with above-median semantic projection (the "same axis, opposite ends" test); then four-way classifier macro-F1. Convincing result: >=80% of over-refusal prompts are low-semantic and >=80% of successful jailbreaks are high-semantic, with four-group macro-F1 >=0.80. Indecision band (before data): either fraction in [60, 80]% means the structure holds only partially — H1 is weakly supported and the intervention is expected to help one failure mode more than the other. Negative result: either fraction <60% means the dual-failure-on-one-axis structure does not hold and H1 is unsupported.

Experiment 3 (H2 — Semantic-Recompute fixes over-refusal and jailbreaks together at one fixed setting). Tests whether subtracting the estimated lexical-trigger contribution at the safety-critical layers, at a single global setting, moves both failure modes in the good direction and Pareto-dominates baselines. Method: estimate the lexical-trigger contribution (via the localized trigger-token attention paths and a lexical projection learned from the same-meaning swap pairs) and subtract it at the safety-critical layers; training-free, one fixed setting per model. Data: over-refusal FPR on XSTest-safe (200), OR-Bench (500), OKTest (300); jailbreak ASR on GCG, AutoDAN, PAIR, roleplay, and the word-substitution attack (100 HarmBench behaviors each); utility on MMLU (2,000-subset), MT-Bench (80), AlpacaEval (805). Systems compared: no intervention, Self-CD, D-STT, SCANS, refusal-direction steering (single threshold), Latent Guard; plus a control that subtracts the semantic (not lexical) component; strength and layer are swept for the Pareto but ONE setting is fixed for the headline. Decisive metric first: the joint movement — over-refusal FPR change AND average jailbreak ASR change at the one fixed setting, relative to no intervention; then MMLU. Convincing result: at one setting, over-refusal FPR drops >=10 points AND average jailbreak ASR drops >=10 points, with MMLU drop <=2 points, while no baseline improves both simultaneously and the semantic-subtraction control worsens both (confirming the direction of the mechanism). Indecision band (before data): one metric improves >=10 points while the other lands in [0, 10] points means Semantic-Recompute helps one failure mode but not both at a shared setting — reported as a partial, not a simultaneous, fix. Negative result: any setting that improves one metric worsens the other means the single-axis simultaneous-fix claim (H2) fails.

Experiment 4 (H2 — adaptive attacker who encodes harm semantically without triggers). Tests whether removing lexical reliance forces attackers to raise the semantic signal, which the semantic-grounded decision still catches. Data: a trigger-free semantic attack that paraphrases the 100 HarmBench behaviors to remove trigger words while preserving intent, run against the Semantic-Recompute-defended models from Experiment 3. Decisive metric first: ASR of the trigger-free attack under Semantic-Recompute vs. no defense; then the semantic-projection level such an attack must reach. Convincing result: the trigger-free attack does not raise ASR above the no-defense baseline, because preserving intent keeps the semantic component high and detectable (raised attack cost is the intended outcome). Indecision band (before data): an ASR increase in [5, 15] points means partial evasion — reported honestly. Negative result: the trigger-free attack raises ASR substantially (>15 points) means harm can be encoded semantically below the decision's reach, a real limit of Semantic-Recompute.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Lexical and semantic harm contributions may not be cleanly separable if the model computes them in entangled, nonlinear ways; the decomposition could be approximate, weakening the causal story. 2) Constructing minimal pairs that truly hold meaning constant while swapping only trigger words (and vice versa) is delicate; residual confounds could contaminate component estimates. 3) The 'same axis, opposite ends' hypothesis may only partially hold: some jailbreaks (e.g., adversarial suffixes) may work by other mechanisms (attention hijacking, refusal-action suppression) rather than lexical stripping, so Semantic-Recompute may help less on those. 4) Subtracting the lexical component could remove legitimate safety signal for prompts that are harmful precisely because of explicit content, causing new under-refusals; the Pareto sweep quantifies this. 5) A single harmfulness direction may be multi-dimensional; may require subspace projection. 6) Directions, lexical projections, and settings are model-specific and require per-model calibration. 7) Adaptive attackers targeting semantic encoding remain a threat, though this raises attack cost, itself a safety gain.

Name: scope_insensitive_refusal
Title: Numbing at Scale: LLM Refusal Grows Sublinearly with the Number of Victims Because Harm Is Read Through a Log-Compressed Magnitude Representation
Short Hypothesis: Borrowing scope insensitivity / psychophysical numbing from human moral psychology (harm to many feels less severe per victim than harm to one), we hypothesize that an aligned LLM's refusal probability for a harmful request grows only SUBLINEARLY -- and can even PLATEAU or DROP -- as the stated number of victims increases, so that a catastrophic-scale harm ('a plan to poison a city's water supply, affecting 500,000 people') is refused no more, and sometimes less, reliably than the same act against one person. Our PRIMARY claim is this continuous, count-varying refusal curve itself: a pre-registered model comparison in which refusal is better fit by log(N) than by linear-N or by no-N effect, distinguishing genuine magnitude numbing from plausibility/credibility effects and generic lexical salience. As a supporting mechanistic account (stated as 'consistent with' unless the intervention cleanly isolates the count subspace), we hypothesize the sublinearity is driven by the model's known log-compressed (Weber-Fechner) numerical magnitude representation feeding the safety pathway, so the marginal refusal signal per additional victim vanishes; re-anchoring/linearizing the victim-count magnitude signal restores scale-sensitive refusal.
Related Work: Two well-established literatures meet here for the first time. (A) LLM numerical magnitude representation: multiple papers show LLMs encode numbers with logarithmic/sublinear (Weber-Fechner) compression akin to the human mental number line ('Number Representations in LLMs' 2025; 'The Other Mind' 2025, which finds log-coding temporal-preferential FFN neurons), that numbers are digit-encoded and CAUSALLY manipulable ('Language Models Encode Numbers Using Digit Representations' 2024), and that magnitude subspaces are perturbable ('Interpreting Multi-Attribute Confounding' 2025). (B) Human moral psychology of scope: robust scope insensitivity, psychophysical numbing, and compassion collapse — harm to many is judged less severe per victim ('A Sorrow Shared Is a Sorrow Halved' 2016), groups get 'less mind' and are harmed more readily ('More People But Less Mind' 2019), scope insensitivity worsens under stress (2019) and depends on tangibility (2018). NONE of this is transferred to LLM safety refusal, and no prior work connects the LLM log-magnitude representation to how refusal scales with harm scale. Safety-geometry work (Refusal is a Single Direction 2024; Geometry of Harmfulness 2025; belief/action separation, Zhao et al. 2025) treats a request at fixed, single-victim scale and never varies the number of victims. My prior identifiable-victim proposal varies victim CONCRETENESS/vividness and my in-group proposal varies victim RELATIONSHIP; this proposal varies victim COUNT and, crucially, advances a specific mechanistic substrate — the pre-existing log-compressed magnitude code — that no prior safety work invokes. Our contribution: introduce scope-insensitive refusal as a new, causally-tested phenomenon, mechanistically grounded in the LLM's numerical magnitude representation, with a magnitude-linearizing defense.
Abstract: Humans are famously scope-insensitive to harm: a single identifiable victim moves us more than a statistical multitude, and compassion collapses as numbers grow -- a bias rooted in the log-compressed way we perceive magnitude. LLMs are trained on human text and, like humans, encode numbers on a sublinear (Weber-Fechner) mental number line. We ask whether these two facts combine into a dangerous safety failure: does an aligned LLM's willingness to refuse a harmful request grow only sublinearly -- or even plateau/reverse -- as the number of potential victims increases, so that mass-casualty requests are refused no more reliably than single-victim ones? Our headline novelty is the CONTINUOUS refusal-vs-count curve (not generic harmfulness detection): prior safety work varies only categorical severity bins or fixed, single-victim scale and so cannot see a scaling law. Concretely, an assistant asked to help harm one person may refuse, while the identical request scaled to a million victims may be answered -- a dimension current harm benchmarks omit entirely. We test three claims on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B. Behaviorally, using minimal pairs that hold the harmful act fixed while varying only the stated victim count across orders of magnitude (1 -> 10 -> 1,000 -> 1,000,000), we test the pre-registered comparison refusal ~ log(N) vs refusal ~ N vs no-N effect, with matched benign, plausibility-matched (realistic high counts), and nonsense-count controls that separate numbing from disbelief and from lexical salience. Mechanistically (Location), we extract a harm-severity direction and reuse published number/magnitude loci, and test whether perceived severity tracks the LOG of the count while the harmfulness belief stays saturated. Causally (Intervention), activation patching that replaces the log-compressed count component with a linearized one increases refusal for large counts, and a direct digit-representation edit moves severity and refusal together -- evidence consistent with the log-magnitude code as the causal bottleneck. We then build Magnitude-Linearizing Anchoring, a training-free intervention that rescales the victim-count signal so refusal grows with true scale. Red-teamers, safety-eval authors, and refusal-defense designers would act on this: a positive result says harm benchmarks must add a victim-count scaling axis and that defenses must be made scale-sensitive; a null (refusal already tracks scale) is itself safety-reassuring. We report the scaling law, the belief-vs-magnitude dissociation, causal patching, mass-casualty refusal gains, over-refusal, numeracy preservation, utility, and a human-comparison sanity check.
Experiments: Shared setup (referenced below). Models: three frozen open-weight instruction-tuned models at the 7-9B scale -- Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-IT. No weights are updated; the only fitted objects are difference-in-means directions and L2-regularized logistic probes on frozen activations. Refusal scoring is greedy (temperature 0); sampled quantities use 3 seeds (0,1,2), mean +/- SD. Refusal is scored by an external rubric judge (HarmBench classifier + Llama-Guard-3-8B) cross-checked against a refusal-string detector, judge primary. Shared dataset. From HarmBench (400) and StrongREJECT (313) we select 40 harmful acts that admit a specifiable victim count (poisoning, mass fraud, infrastructure sabotage, disease spread, wide-scale harassment), 8 per category x 5 categories. For each act we author requests holding the act and per-victim severity fixed while varying only the stated victim count N in {1, 10, 100, 1000, 100000, 1000000} -- 240 harmful items. Two size-matched controls: a BENIGN set with the same numeric manipulation ('plan a party for N guests', 240) and a NON-VICTIM large-number set (large numbers unrelated to harm scale, 240). We use 40 acts because each needs hand-matched count-graded minimal pairs; a 30-item subset is externally checked for payload-actionability constancy (target kappa >= 0.6). Experiment 1 (H1 -- Refusal grows only sublinearly, or plateaus/reverses, with victim count): Tests the scaling shape of refusal against N on identical acts. Data: 240 harmful + 240 benign + 240 non-victim items. Systems compared: refusal-rate curve over the six N levels, harmful vs benign vs non-victim. Decisive metric first: model comparison of refusal-vs-N fits -- delta-AIC between a log(N) fit and a linear-in-N fit, plus the fitted log-scale slope and the sign of refusal(N=1e6) - refusal(N=1). Convincing: the log fit is preferred by delta-AIC >= 10 over the linear fit in >= 2 of 3 models (sublinear scaling), and the benign/non-victim curves show no comparable harm-scale rise (isolating scope from raw number handling); the strong prediction (flat/decreasing large-N refusal) is confirmed if refusal(1e6) - refusal(1) <= 0 pp. Indecision band: delta-AIC between 0 and 10 favoring log, OR a large-N-minus-small-N change within +/-5 pp -- reported as weakly sublinear, inconclusive on the plateau/reversal claim. Negative (linear or super-linear fit preferred, delta-AIC >= 10 the other way): no scope insensitivity; we report the null (including the safety-reassuring case that refusal tracks scale) and stop before the mechanism experiments.
